About this simulation

On screen
Top: the star, drawn at a fixed size in its black-body colour, and its visible spectrum from 380 to 700 nm with the Balmer lines Hα, Hβ, Hγ and Hδ, each as dark as the relative Balmer strength. Bottom: against T from 3000 to 25 000 K, the share of all hydrogen in k = 2 divided by its maximum, the neutral fraction nI/(nI+nII) (left axis, linear) and the share of neutral atoms in k = 2, n2/nI (right axis, logarithmic), traced only where you have been, with the spectral classes along the top and the Sun marked at 5772 K.
Controls
Temperature, 3000 to 25 000 K: drag it, use the chips, or press Sweep to carry it up to 25 000 K at 1100 K per second. Electron pressure Pe, 2 to 200 N m⁻² on a logarithmic scale, with chips for 2, 20 and 200 N m⁻²: changing it clears the traced curves and keeps the previous product curve as a faint dashed reference.
Measured
Boltzmann populations of the levels k = 1 and 2 (g = 2k²), Saha ionisation with ZI = 2, ZII = 1 and ne = Pe/kBT; Balmer strength = n2/(nI+nII) divided by its maximum over 3000 to 25 000 K at the same Pe. Very small fractions are shown in powers of ten.
Model limits
Only the levels k = 1 and 2 enter the partition function, which is accurate at these temperatures. The electron pressure is held fixed while T changes; in real stars it changes along the spectral sequence, which is one reason the observed Balmer maximum, in early A stars, sits near 9500 K. The darkness of the drawn lines follows the number of absorbing atoms only, with no line-formation physics, and the star is drawn at a fixed size.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Excited atoms as it heats

Set the electron pressure to 20 N m−2 and the temperature to 5800 K, close to that of the Sun. Before dragging the temperature up to 9000 K, predict how the fraction n2/nI of neutral atoms in the level k = 2 will change.

2 · Stripping the electrons

Keep the electron pressure at 20 N m−2 and the temperature at 5800 K. The ionisation energy of hydrogen corresponds to χH/kB ≈ 158 000 K. Before sweeping the temperature upwards, predict at what temperature the neutral fraction will fall to one half.

3 · Hotter still

Keep the electron pressure at 20 N m−2 and set the temperature to 10 000 K. Between here and 25 000 K the Boltzmann fraction n2/nI grows more than a thousandfold. Before dragging the temperature up to 25 000 K, predict what happens to the Balmer lines.

4 · How many atoms are excited

Keep the electron pressure at 20 N m−2 and set the temperature to 9900 K, close to the peak. Before reading the last readout, predict what fraction of all the hydrogen is in the level k = 2, where the Balmer lines are darkest.

5 · Raising the pressure

Keep the temperature at 9900 K and raise the electron pressure to 200 N m−2, ten times the typical value. Before sweeping the temperature again, predict where the peak of the Balmer lines will move.

6 · Why the lines peak

A Balmer line needs neutral hydrogen already excited to k = 2. Heating raises the excited share (Boltzmann) but also strips the electrons off (Saha), and the product peaks near 104 K, in the A stars.

Cool stars have too few excited atoms, hot stars too few neutral ones. So the strength of a line tracks the temperature, not the amount of hydrogen: the Sun has as much hydrogen as Vega, but much weaker Balmer lines.

01

At a glance

Stars of different temperatures show Balmer lines of very different strength. This sim shows how a star's temperature and electron pressure set how many hydrogen atoms can absorb in those lines, and so how dark the lines are.

What you'll learn

  • What a hydrogen atom needs to absorb in a Balmer line.
  • How temperature and electron pressure change the number of atoms that can.
  • How that number sets how dark the lines are drawn.
The sim's layout: the star and spectrum on top, the empty plot below.

What's on screen

  • Top: the star at its temperature and spectral class, and its spectrum from 380 to 700 nm with Hα, Hβ, Hγ and Hδ marked, each line drawn as dark as the relative strength.
  • Bottom: three curves against T, traced where you have been. Orange: n2/nI, on the right-hand log axis. Violet: the neutral fraction. Cyan: the strength.
  • Along the plot: the spectral classes at the top and the Sun at 5772 K. Readouts repeat the numbers.

03

Balmer lines need atoms already in k = 2

The Balmer series is every transition that ends on the level k = 2. In a star the lines appear in absorption, so a photon can be absorbed only by a neutral atom that is already in k = 2.

The strength of the lines therefore follows the share of all the hydrogen, neutral and ionised, that is in k = 2. It is a product of two fractions (3.13):

The notes' (3.13). The sim's three readouts, Excited, Neutral and their product.

Here nI and nII are the number densities of neutral atoms and of ions, and n2 that of atoms in k = 2. The Boltzmann equation sets the first fraction and the Saha equation the second.

The sim keeps k = 1 and k = 2, with g1 = 2 and g2 = 8, so nI ≈ n1 + n2. It draws each line as dark as the relative strength: n2/(nI+nII) divided by its greatest value at the same Pe.

Key idea. The lines can be no stronger than the number of neutral atoms in k = 2.
See itSet T = 9900 K at Pe = 20 N m−2 and read the three numbers. Watch for: the product row, n2/(nI+nII), equal to the Excited row times the Neutral row.
04

The excited share rises steeply with temperature

For the levels k = 2 and k = 1, with E2 − E1 = ¾χH = 10.2 eV, the Boltzmann equation gives (3.5)

The notes' (3.5).

Here χH = 13.6 eV is the ionisation energy of hydrogen, and χH/kB = 1.58 × 105 K. The sim's Excited readout is n2/nI, which equals n2/n1 divided by 1 + n2/n1, and the two agree while n2/n1 is small.

The exponent ¾χH/kBT is large and changes fast. At 5800 K it is 20.4 and n2/nI is 5.4 × 10−9. At 9000 K it is 13.2 and n2/nI is 7.7 × 10−6, 1400 times larger. By 25 000 K the exponent is 4.7 and n2/nI is 0.034. Pe does not appear.

Key idea. On its own the Boltzmann equation makes the excited share rise all the way from 3000 to 25 000 K.
The sim's Excited readout against T, on a logarithmic axis. The same at every Pe.
See itSet T = 9000 K. At 5800 K the Excited readout is 5.44 × 10−9. Watch for: the readout at 7.73 × 10−6 and the orange dot high on the right-hand log axis.
05

Ionisation sets in far below kBT = χH

Hydrogen also ionises, H I ⇌ H II + e−, and an ion has no level k = 2. The Saha equation gives, with the electron pressure Pe = nekBT (3.12),

The notes' (3.12).

The sim takes 𝒵I = 2 and 𝒵II = 1, so 2𝒵II/𝒵I = 1. The exponential favours the atom, since ionising costs χH. The factor (2πmekBT/h2)3/2/ne favours ionisation: it counts the states open to a freed electron, and it is very large.

So the hydrogen ionises while kBT is still far below χH. At 20 N m−2 the neutral fraction nI/(nI+nII) falls to one half at 9560 K, where kBT = χH/16.5. It goes from 0.975 at 8000 K to 0.019 at 12 000 K.

Key idea. Ionisation turns on over a few thousand kelvin, at a temperature far below the one where kBT = χH.
The sim's Neutral readout against T at Pe = 20 N m−2.
See itSet T = 9560 K at Pe = 20 N m−2. Watch for: the Neutral readout at about 0.50, and the violet dot on the half-way line of the plot.
06

The strength peaks near 10 000 K

Below about 8000 K nearly all the hydrogen is neutral, so the product follows the rising excited share. Higher up the neutral fraction falls faster than that share rises, and the product falls.

At 20 N m−2 the product n2/(nI+nII) is greatest near 9880 K, in class A (7500 to 10 000 K). At 9900 K the Excited readout is 2.55 × 10−5, the Neutral readout 0.34, and the product 8.7 × 10−6: about one hydrogen atom in 105 is in k = 2.

At 25 000 K the Excited readout has grown to 0.034, 1200 times its value at 10 000 K, but the Neutral readout is 3.4 × 10−6. The strength is 1.3 per cent of its peak.

07

Raising the electron pressure moves the peak up only a little

A proton meets free electrons, and recombines, more often in a denser gas. In the Saha equation Pe stands in the denominator, so at any T the ratio nII/nI is inversely proportional to Pe. The Boltzmann fraction does not depend on Pe at all.

The temperature enters through an exponential, so a large change in Pe is made up by a small change in T. Between 2, 20 and 200 N m−2 the half-ionisation temperature runs about 8500, 9600 and 10 900 K, and the peak about 8800, 9900 and 11 200 K. Each tenfold step moves the peak by about a thousand kelvin.

At 200 N m−2 the peak lies in class B in the sim's classes. In real stars Pe changes along the spectral sequence, which is one reason the observed maximum sits near 9500 K, in the early A stars.

Key idea. Pressure shifts the maximum; it does not remove it.
The strength at Pe = 2 (dashed), 20 (solid) and 200 N m−2 (dotted), each relative to its own greatest value.
See itSet Pe = 200 N m−2 and trace the run through the peak. Watch for: the cyan peak line labelled peak 11233 K, to the right of the faint dashed curve left by 20 N m−2.
08

Where it matters, from spectral classes to abundances

  • Sorting stars. The spectral sequence O B A F G K M is a sequence in temperature. The Balmer lines are weak in O, stronger in B, strongest in A, then weaker through F, G and K. Temperature, not the amount of hydrogen, sets that pattern.
  • Counting atoms. Payne used the Boltzmann and Saha equations in 1925 to turn the strengths of the lines of each element into the numbers of its atoms. Calcium, with χ ≈ 6.1 eV, is mostly singly ionised in G and K stars, and its Ca II lines are strongest there.
  • Giants and dwarfs. A giant's atmosphere has a lower pressure than a main-sequence star's, so an element is more highly ionised at the same temperature.
09

Summary

In one line. This sim shows how a star's temperature and electron pressure set the strength of the Balmer lines of hydrogen.
  • A Balmer line needs a neutral atom already in k = 2, so the strength follows n2/(nI+nII) = (n2/nI) × nI/(nI+nII).
  • The Boltzmann factor makes n2/nI rise with T; the Saha equation makes the neutral fraction fall, at a T far below kBT = χH.
  • The product peaks near 10 000 K, and a tenfold rise in Pe moves the peak up by about a thousand kelvin.

Common mix-ups

  • "The hottest stars have the strongest hydrogen lines." At 25 000 K the strength is 1.3 per cent of its peak, at 20 N m−2.
  • "Hydrogen ionises when kBT reaches 13.6 eV." Half is ionised near 9560 K, where kBT is χH/16.5: a freed electron has many states open to it.
  • "The lines fade because hot atoms stop being excited." The excited share keeps rising. What falls is the number of neutral atoms.

Things to try on your own

  • At each of the three pressures, find the temperature where the Neutral readout is 0.50 and the temperature of the peak, and compare them.
  • Sweep T at each pressure and note the class where the lines are darkest.
